packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for 'downstream' default effects, synthesizing when defaults' immediate effects persist, fade, or reverse across subsequent consumer decisions.
packets.methodology: Conceptual review and theoretical framework paper synthesizing the consumer default-effect literature. Abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a general model for predicting whether our round-up default's initial enrollment lift will persist or decay, and what factors moderate that — directly informs how we should measure success beyond signup, not just enrollment rate.
limitations: theoretical/conceptual, not a new empirical estimate
not specific to financial products
abstract gives no effect sizes
packets.relevance_reason: General consumer-behavior framework for downstream default persistence, matching the brief's core question of whether the enrollment lift lasts at 6-12 months.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges produced medium-to-large effects on investment risk-taking but also lowered ratings of the wealth manager's advice — especially when the default was refused — with perceived honesty mediating the effect.
packets.methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative multi-country European survey experiment (n=4207) on default-framed investment allocation.
packets.why_it_matters: Direct EU evidence that defaults can be perceived as less trustworthy or manipulative when refused, and that presentation framing shifts the level people choose — bears squarely on both the reputational-risk and anchoring questions the brief raises for the round-up entry and level decisions.
limitations: investment risk allocation setting, not round-up savings specifically
one-shot experimental ratings, no field or behavioral persistence data
packets.relevance_reason: EU-based experimental evidence on default effect size, level framing/anchoring, and perceived manipulation — matches nearly every open question in the brief for a consumer financial-advice context.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and default auto-escalation: steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of employees escalate on their first scheduled date.
packets.methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans accounting for job separation, withdrawal at separation, and auto-escalation opt-out.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of our support team's objection: the enrollment lift is real at signup but its effect on actual saving shrinks dramatically over time — directly bearing on whether opt-out enrollment is a vanity metric.
limitations: retirement 401(k) plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated setting
packets.relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving long-term, exactly the persistence evidence the brief asked for.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the autopay-minimum option reduced minimum-only payers by 23% but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, with nudged cardholders enrolling autopay at only slightly above the minimum.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on credit cards with 6-month follow-up using administrative payment data.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly evidences the support team's fear: a nudge that shifts nominal enrollment/payment behavior does not change the underlying financial outcome — critical to whether opt-out enrollment changes real saving or just who is nominally enrolled.
limitations: Credit card debt paydown, not savings enrollment
no data beyond 6 months
not a savings-app setting
packets.relevance_reason: Consumer financial product with liquid dynamics (credit card) showing default/nudge effects on nominal enrollment diverge from effects on the real financial outcome — the exact caution the brief raises about the round-up feature.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: At-scale field experiments automatically enrolling U.K. bank customers into just-in-time overdraft text alerts reduced unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in market-wide annual savings, though alerts captured less than half of potential avoidable savings.
packets.methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments run directly through major U.K. retail banks' own apps/systems.
packets.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that automatic (opt-out-style) enrollment into a bank-app feature works at scale without an employer intermediary, directly supporting the feasibility case for opt-out entry into the round-up feature in the same consumer-banking channel.
limitations: measures a different feature (alerts, not savings enrollment)
no data on retention or amounts saved over 6-12 months
packets.relevance_reason: Same industry and delivery channel as the product being built, showing a consumer-bank automatic-enrollment default working at scale without employer trust as the mechanism.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: A structural model decomposing default adherence into deviation cost and opt-out cost, estimated on 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions, finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions, and that adding an intermediate preset option (15%) captures 69% of achievable welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
packets.methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6 million real tipping transactions plus a stated-preference survey, with counterfactual menu-design simulations.
packets.why_it_matters: Its friction-decomposition method and menu-redesign counterfactual transfer directly to our preset multiplier decision: it shows how adding an intermediate preset level between existing options can capture most of the achievable welfare gain without changing underlying frictions — directly actionable for deciding among 1x/2x/5x and which to pre-select.
limitations: tipping decisions, not financial savings
single deviation-cost/opt-out-cost model may not capture savings-specific psychology
no persistence or withdrawal outcomes measured
packets.relevance_reason: Explicit structural method for how preset menu options anchor choices and how welfare gains from menu redesign are quantified — a direct method transfer to the round-up multiplier preset-level decision despite the differing product.
packets.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
packets.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

packets.key_finding: Maps EU laws on dark patterns and develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence from manipulative practices, including pre-selected defaults.
packets.methodology: Legal-doctrinal analysis and normative taxonomy construction; abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly frames when an opt-out default for the round-up feature would read as a lawful nudge versus a regulated dark pattern under EU law, which should shape how the entry decision and its exit mechanism are designed and disclosed.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not an empirical estimate of enrollment or savings effects
no financial-product-specific case studies given in the abstract
packets.relevance_reason: Gives the EU regulatory yardstick for judging whether the chosen default design (especially opt-out) risks being classified as manipulative.
packets.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
packets.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.

packets.key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is highly insensitive even to substantial losses from staying with a bad default, with active-choice variation driven by transitory shocks rather than attentiveness.
packets.methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options among low-income Medicare beneficiaries.
packets.why_it_matters: Shows default persistence can be extremely strong and largely insensitive to outcome value — a caution against assuming our round-up default's effect will fade the way the retirement literature suggests, and a warning that passivity can mask real harm for those defaulted badly.
limitations: health insurance/drug benefit setting, not consumer savings
government administrative program, not a self-directed app
no financial contribution-amount analogy
packets.relevance_reason: Strong, persistent default-effect evidence with a distributional focus on low-income beneficiaries, relevant to the brief's concern about who is helped or hurt by defaults, despite the different domain.
packets.title: The Behavioral Foundations of Default Effects: Theory and Evidence from Medicare Part D
packets.abstract: We show in two natural experiments that default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization of low-income beneficiaries. The implications of this phenomenon for welfare and optimal policy depend on the sensitivity of passivity to the value of the default option. Using random assignment to default options, we show that beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive, even when enrolling in the default option would result in substantial drug consumption losses. A third natural experiment suggests that variation in active choice is driven by random transitory shocks rather than the inherent attentiveness of some beneficiaries.

packets.key_finding: Synthesizes household-finance evidence across savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance, and reviews interventions including choice architecture and product design used to shape financial behavior.
packets.methodology: Narrative review/handbook chapter synthesizing the behavioral household finance literature; abstract gives no pooled effect sizes.
packets.why_it_matters: Provides a broad, current synthesis of which choice-architecture levers (including defaults) reliably move household financial behavior versus which do not, useful as a sanity check against over-relying on a single default-effect study.
limitations: narrative overview, not a systematic review with pooled effect sizes
covers household finance broadly rather than round-up/micro-savings apps specifically
packets.relevance_reason: The review/synthesis anchor the brief asks for, spanning several of the exact mechanisms (defaults, product design, choice architecture) the two decisions depend on.
packets.title: Behavioral Household Finance
packets.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

packets.key_finding: In a Brazilian fintech field experiment, payment reminders cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised checking-account overdraft fees by 9%, concentrated among users with a history of overdraft use, so overdraft-prone users saw a net 5% increase in fees while everyone else saved 15%.
packets.methodology: Randomized field experiment on a consumer financial-management platform in Brazil.
packets.why_it_matters: Shows directly, in a comparable consumer fintech setting, that a well-intentioned nudge can help most users while actively harming a vulnerable subgroup — the exact distributional failure mode the brief warns against building unknowingly.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrollment defaults or round-up savings specifically
single-country, single-platform sample
packets.relevance_reason: A consumer fintech RCT demonstrating heterogeneous, sometimes harmful, effects of a nudge, directly supporting the brief's concern about who is helped versus hurt by design defaults.
packets.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
packets.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

alternates.key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at three firms, but ~80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half still did after three years, roughly offsetting the accumulation gains from higher participation.
alternates.methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large firms comparing pre- and post-automatic-enrollment cohorts.
alternates.why_it_matters: The founding demonstration that a preset default level strongly anchors behavior for years, and that anchoring at a poorly chosen default can cancel out the participation gains from auto-enrollment — exactly the risk in shipping a pre-selected round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer 401(k) plans with employer-selected defaults, not a self-directed consumer app
predates the fintech/mobile and EU dark-pattern regulatory context the brief cares about
alternates.relevance_reason: The classic evidence that anchoring at a preset default level can offset the enrollment benefit of a default — directly on point for whether to pre-select a multiplier and which one.
alternates.title: For Better or For Worse: Default Effects and 401(k) Savings Behavior
alternates.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan. Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation. We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so. As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle. We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund). Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund. The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward. While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation. In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average. However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

alternates.key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic (passive) employer contributions raised total saving substantially, while tax subsidies requiring active choice mostly just shifted assets between accounts, with each $1 of subsidy raising saving by only 1 cent; ~85% of people are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but moved by defaults.
alternates.methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data for the full Danish population, comparing active-choice subsidy policies to passive default-contribution policies.
alternates.why_it_matters: The classic large-sample demonstration that passive/default mechanisms move far more people than active-choice incentives, and that responsiveness differs sharply between financially sophisticated 'active' and unsophisticated 'passive' individuals — a distributional pattern the round-up team should expect to see mirrored.
limitations: Danish retirement/tax-advantaged account system, not a consumer banking app
government subsidy policy rather than a private-app choice-architecture decision
alternates.relevance_reason: Foundational large-N evidence on the passive/active saver split and the outsized effect of defaults over active-choice incentives, the empirical backbone much later fintech work argues with.
alternates.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
alternates.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.

alternates.key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains attenuate substantially between 12 and 36 months, though it still reduces inequality in savings; a life-cycle model estimates the effective switching cost at about $250.
alternates.methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly quantifies the persistence question the brief asks about — default gains shrink over medium-run horizons — while showing defaults reduce inequality in savings, a distributional benefit to weigh against disengagement costs.
limitations: employer/national retirement plans, not a consumer app
36-month horizon still shorter than a full career
not a liquid consumer product
alternates.relevance_reason: Best available quantification of default-effect attenuation over time in the closest analogous (retirement) literature, central to the brief's persistence question.
alternates.title: Default Options and Retirement Saving Dynamics
alternates.abstract: Using data from over 100 US retirement plans and a representative UK panel, I document the impact of auto-enrollment (AE) on retirement savings at different horizons. I replicate the impact of AE on participation and contributions in the short run (at 12 months), but I show that these gains are attenuated over the medium run (at 36 months). At this longer horizon, the average savings increases are modest, though AE significantly lowers inequality in savings. To assess AE’s lifetime impact, I estimate a life cycle consumption-savings model that can fit the observed patterns with a switching cost of approximately $250, smaller than previous estimates. (JEL D15, G51, J26, J32)

alternates.key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment raised participation above 85% at three firms, but roughly 80% of participants anchored on the low default savings rate and conservative default fund, with half still at the default after three years.
alternates.methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans.
alternates.why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a preset default level strongly anchors contribution-rate choices — the core precedent behind our concern that a preset round-up multiplier will anchor most users at that level rather than a higher one.
limitations: classic, dated employer 401(k) study with no publication year given
employer-mediated trust relationship does not carry to a consumer app
no comparison to opt-in or active choice
alternates.relevance_reason: Foundational anchoring-on-default-level finding that the current literature (and this brief) continues to argue with; directly informs the round-up multiplier preset decision despite the different setting.
alternates.title: Perspectives on the Economics of Aging
alternates.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan.Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation.We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so.As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle.We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund).Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund.The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward.While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation.In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average.However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

alternates.key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had opted out by 12 months (versus ~50% opt-out at lower defaults in the literature), but many who stayed at the default were contributing a likely-suboptimal amount, especially lower earners.
alternates.methodology: Administrative panel data from a single employer plan with a high default, compared against a literature review of lower-default plans.
alternates.why_it_matters: Shows that raising a default's level changes opt-out behavior and strongly anchors people at the preset value even when it is a poor fit for them — directly relevant to choosing which round-up multiplier to pre-select.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app the user chose
no employer-as-intermediary comparison to isolate what carries over to fintech
alternates.relevance_reason: Empirically quantifies how a preset default level anchors contribution amounts, bearing on the multiplier pre-selection decision.
alternates.title: Automatic Enrollment with a 12% Default Contribution Rate
alternates.abstract: We study a retirement savings plan with a default contribution rate of 12% of income, which is much higher than previously studied defaults. Twenty-five percent of employees had not opted out of this default 12 months after hire; a literature review finds that the corresponding fraction in plans with lower defaults is approximately one-half. Because only contributions above 12% were matched by the employer, 12% was likely to be a suboptimal contribution rate for employees. Employees who remained at the 12% default contribution rate had average income that was approximately one-third lower than would be predicted from the relationship between salaries and contribution rates among employees who were not at 12%. Defaults may influence low-income employees more strongly in part because these employees face higher psychological barriers to active decision making.
